c.tagline: Lakeside capital where volcanoes and history meet.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis are unmetered; agree on the fare (in córdobas) with the driver before getting in. Only use officially registered taxis, identifiable by a red stripe on the license plate.

emergency.note: Tourist hotline 101 (Claro mobile). Response times can be slow; use only officially marked red-striped taxis.

avoid.reason: Caution around the Mercado Oriental and at night

hood_desc: Leafy, embassy-lined residential district with quiet streets, boutique guesthouses and upscale restaurants; suits first-time visitors, business travelers and couples wanting a calm, central base.
Managua's commercial heart around the Metrocentro mall with malls, banks and chain hotels; suits business travelers and anyone wanting maximum convenience and easy transit access.
Modern strip of newer apartments, gyms, cafes and the Galerías Santo Domingo mall heading toward Masaya; suits digital nomads, families and longer-stay visitors with a car.

Historic district on the hill near Tiscapa Lagoon and Plaza Inter, home to the iconic pyramid-shaped former Intercontinental (now Crowne Plaza) and government buildings; suits history buffs and those wanting central, landmark-adjacent lodging.
lodging: Los Robles Charming Colonial Boutique Hotel

water.note: Avoid tap water; drink only bottled or purified water.

transit.pay: Fares on city buses are paid in cash (córdobas) directly to the driver or a fare collector on board; there is no rechargeable transit card. Taxis are typically negotiated up front since few are metered.
transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5:00am-10:00pm; limited service after dark, so taxis are the norm at night.
transit.note: Public buses are crowded, poorly marked and not recommended for tourists unfamiliar with the routes; licensed radio taxis are the practical option for visitors.

tip.r: Tipping isn't obligatory; 10% is appreciated at sit-down restaurants if a service charge isn't already included.

food.name: Gallo pinto
food.desc: Nicaragua's breakfast staple: day-old rice fried with small red beans, onion and sweet pepper, served with eggs, cuajada cheese and fried plantain.

places.name: La Cocina de Dona Haydee
places.note: Managua's best-known traditional Nicaraguan kitchen; the standard for classic pinto breakfasts.

places.name: Mercado Roberto Huembes comedores
places.note: Rows of market cooks serving pinto with eggs and cuajada from early morning.

places.name: Puerto Salvador Allende
places.note: Waterfront strip of Nicaraguan restaurants doing pinto plates all day.

food.name: Nacatamal
food.desc: Sunday-morning giant tamal: corn masa with pork, rice, potato, mint and chilli wrapped in plantain leaf and steamed for hours.

places.name: La Cocina de Dona Haydee
places.note: Serves proper weekend nacatamales with pickled onion and bread on the side.

places.name: Mercado Roberto Huembes
places.note: Market cooks sell nacatamales by the leaf-wrapped bundle, best on Saturday and Sunday.

places.name: Puerto Salvador Allende
places.note: Several stalls keep nacatamales steaming through the weekend evenings.

food.name: Vigoron
food.desc: Boiled yuca topped with crunchy chicharron and a vinegary cabbage-and-tomato curtido, piled on a banana leaf and eaten by hand.

places.name: Mercado Roberto Huembes
places.note: Classic market setting for vigoron; cheap, generous and freshly fried chicharron.

places.name: La Cocina de Dona Haydee
places.note: Sit-down version with reliable hygiene if you would rather skip a market bench.

places.name: Puerto Salvador Allende
places.note: Easy place to try vigoron alongside other Nicaraguan street classics.

food.name: Quesillo
food.desc: A warm corn tortilla wrapped around soft stringy cheese, pickled onions, cream and salt, served in a plastic bag you drink from at the end.

places.name: Roadside quesillo stands, Carretera Nueva a Leon
places.note: The La Paz Centro road is the traditional quesillo run out of Managua.

places.name: Mercado Roberto Huembes
places.note: In-town option; quesillos made to order with plenty of crema.

places.name: Puerto Salvador Allende
places.note: Kiosks sell quesillos and cacao drinks along the lakefront promenade.

food.name: Baho
food.desc: Slow-steamed layers of beef, green and ripe plantain and yuca cooked in banana leaves, served with cabbage salad. A weekend family dish.

places.name: La Cocina de Dona Haydee
places.note: One of the few sit-down restaurants that reliably has baho on the menu.

places.name: Mercado Roberto Huembes
places.note: Market comedores serve baho at weekends, ladled straight from the pot.

places.name: Mercado Oriental food stalls
places.note: Huge working market with cheap baho and indio viejo at lunchtime.

food.name: Carne asada and churrasco
food.desc: Thin marinated beef grilled over wood, plated with gallo pinto, fried cheese, plantain and chimichurri. Nicaragua's go-to celebration meal.

places.name: Los Ranchos
places.note: Long-standing Managua steak institution, a local favourite for grilled beef.

places.name: Don Candido
places.note: Upmarket grill regularly listed among the city's best for quality meat.

places.name: La Plancha
places.note: Popular Nicaraguan grill chain; big churrasco plates at moderate prices.

food.name: Macua cocktail
food.desc: Nicaragua's national cocktail: Flor de Cana white rum shaken with guava and lemon juice over ice. Flor de Cana aged rums are worth trying neat.

places.name: Don Candido
places.note: Good bar list and properly made macuas with aged Flor de Cana available.

places.name: Puerto Salvador Allende
places.note: Lakefront bars pour macuas at sunset with live music at weekends.

places.name: Los Ranchos
places.note: Old-school setting for a rum cocktail before a grilled-beef dinner.

food.name: Pinolillo and cacao con leche
food.desc: Pinolillo is toasted corn and cacao whisked with milk or water; cacao con leche is its richer cousin. Both are drunk cold, all day.

places.name: Mercado Roberto Huembes
places.note: Market drink stalls blend pinolillo and cacao fresh in front of you.

places.name: La Cocina de Dona Haydee
places.note: Serves pinolillo and other refrescos naturales with traditional plates.

places.name: Puerto Salvador Allende
places.note: Kiosks along the promenade sell chilled cacao and tiste by the cup.

landmarks: Old Cathedral of Managua (Catedral Vieja)
Left dramatically in ruins since the devastating 1972 earthquake, this crumbling neoclassical cathedral stands as a haunting, iconic symbol of Managua's turbulent history.
Loma de Tiscapa
This hilltop park overlooking a volcanic crater lake features a giant silhouette statue of revolutionary hero Augusto Sandino and sweeping panoramic views of Managua.
Puerto Salvador Allende
This lively lakeside boardwalk on Lake Xolotlán buzzes with restaurants, amusement rides, and colorful sculptures, making it Managua's favorite spot for an evening out.
National Palace of Culture
This grand neoclassical palace on the old Plaza de la Revolución once housed the government and now holds the National Museum, showcasing Nicaragua's art and pre-Columbian artifacts.
Árboles de la Vida (Trees of Life)
Rows of towering, brightly lit metal tree sculptures line Managua's Avenida Bolívar, creating a surreal, colorful spectacle that has become a beloved civic emblem.
Plaza de la Revolución
This historic central plaza, framed by the ruined old cathedral and national palace, has been the stage for major political rallies and events throughout Nicaragua's modern history.
Malecón de Managua
This lakefront promenade along Lake Xolotlán offers cooling breezes, food stalls, and views toward the distant Momotombo volcano across the water.
Rubén Darío National Theatre
Nicaragua's premier performing arts venue hosts opera, ballet, and symphony performances in an elegant modernist building named for the country's celebrated poet.
Metropolitan Cathedral of Managua
Designed with dozens of small domes resembling an egg carton, this striking modern cathedral built after the 1972 quake is one of the city's most distinctive architectural landmarks.
Huellas de Acahualinca
This small but fascinating archaeological site preserves ancient footprints pressed into volcanic mud roughly 6,000 years ago, among the oldest human traces in Central America.

train.note: Nicaragua has no railway - the national rail network was dismantled in the 1990s. Travel is by coach or car.

intl.to: San José & Panama City, plus Tegucigalpa, San Salvador & Guatemala City (+ Tapachula, Mexico)

bus.note: Tica Bus links Managua to every Central American capital and on to Tapachula, Mexico; Transnica and Nicabus focus on the popular Managua-San José (Costa Rica) run. Carry your passport for the Peñas Blancas and other border stops.

ferry.note: No international passenger ferries run from Managua. Nicaragua's passenger boats are domestic, on Lake Nicaragua - ferries from San Jorge/Rivas to Ometepe Island and the long Granada-San Carlos lake service.

half.name: León
half.blurb: Historic Nicaraguan city known for colonial churches, colorful streets, and revolutionary murals.

half.name: Chinandega
half.blurb: Nicaraguan city known for sugarcane fields and nearby volcanoes.

half.name: Matagalpa
half.blurb: Mountain city in Nicaragua's highlands known for its coffee farms and cool climate.

full.name: Tegucigalpa
full.blurb: Mountain-ringed capital of Honduras known for colonial architecture and hillside neighborhoods.

full.name: San Miguel
full.blurb: Eastern Salvadoran city known for its lively carnival and volcanic backdrop.

full.name: Liberia
full.blurb: Northern Costa Rican city known as a gateway to Guanacaste's beaches and volcanoes.

full.name: Bluefields
full.blurb: Caribbean coast town known for its Afro-Caribbean and Creole cultural heritage.
